section_title: 1. Definition and Binary Search Tree Invariant
text: A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a hierarchical binary tree data structure where each node contains a key, and satisfies the binary search invariant: for any node N, all keys in N's left subtree are strictly less than N.key, and all keys in N's right subtree are strictly greater than N.key (assuming unique keys).

Recursive Insertion: To insert value x into tree rooted at root:
1. If root is None, return TreeNode(x).
2. If x < root.val, recursively insert into root.left: root.left = insert(root.left, x).
3. If x > root.val, recursively insert into root.right: root.right = insert(root.right, x).
4. Return root.

> root.val, recursively insert into root.right: root.right = insert(root.right, x).
4. Return root.

Lookup / Search: Starting at root, compare target key with current node value. If equal, node is found. If target < root.val, traverse left; if target > root.val, traverse right. If null pointer is reached, key does not exist.

Note on Self-Balancing Trees: To prevent O(n) degeneration when inserting sorted data, self-balancing BSTs such as AVL Trees or Red-Black Trees maintain a balance factor using tree rotations, guaranteeing O(log n) worst-case height.

Black Trees maintain a balance factor using tree rotations, guaranteeing O(log n) worst-case height.

Table Data:
| Operation | Average Case (Balanced) | Worst Case (Degenerate / Skewed) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Search | O(log n) | O(n) - Skewed linked list |
| Insertion | O(log n) | O(n) - Skewed linked list |
| Deletion | O(log n) | O(n) - Skewed linked list |
| In-Order Traversal | O(n) | O(n) - Sorted order output |
